question: The lecture states that a continuous function is a morphism between topological spaces. Explain how the fact that \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) ensures that \(f\) preserves the closeness of points in the domain and codomain, and why this is a key property of continuous maps.
answer: A morphism between topological spaces preserves the structure of open sets: if a set is open in the domain, its image is open in the codomain. The condition \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) means that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). This is exactly the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition of continuity, which guarantees that points that are close in the domain map to points that are close in the codomain. Hence the convergence of the modulus of continuity ensures that \(f\) preserves closeness, a fundamental property of continuous maps.

question: It is mentioned that the convergence of \(\omega_f(\eta)\) to zero as \(\eta\to0\) is crucial for proving the existence of the Riemann integral for continuous functions on a closed, bounded interval. Describe the logical steps that connect this convergence property to the ability to approximate the integral by Riemann sums.
answer: To approximate the Riemann integral of a continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\), one partitions the interval into subintervals of width at most \(\eta\). The Riemann sum uses sample points \(x_i\) in each subinterval. The error between the integral and the Riemann sum can be bounded by the sum of \(\omega_f(\eta)\) over all subintervals. Since \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\), by choosing a partition fine enough (small \(\eta\)), the total error can be made arbitrarily small. Thus the convergence of \(\omega_f(\eta)\) to zero guarantees that the Riemann sums converge to the integral, establishing its existence for continuous functions on closed, bounded intervals.

question: How does the fact that the modulus of continuity of the linear function \(f(x)=ax+b\) equals \(|a|\eta\) illustrate the general principle that \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) for any continuous function, and why does this imply that \(f\) is uniformly continuous on a closed interval?
answer: For \(f(x)=ax+b\), \(\omega_f(\eta)=|a|\eta\) because the maximum difference occurs when \(x\) and \(y\) are at the endpoints of an interval of length \(\eta\).  Since \(|a|\eta\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\), this shows that the modulus of continuity vanishes for this specific continuous function.  The same reasoning applies to any continuous function: continuity guarantees that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\).  Taking the supremum over all such pairs with \(|x-y|\le\eta\) yields \(\omega_f(\eta)\le\varepsilon\) whenever \(\eta<\delta\), so \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\).  On a closed interval, this uniform bound for all \(x,y\) shows that \(f\) is uniformly continuous.

question: Given that the modulus of continuity is defined as a supremum over all \(|f(x)-f(y)|\) with \(|x-y|\le\eta\), justify why the property \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) follows from the definition of continuity of \(f\).
answer: The modulus \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is the least upper bound of the set \(\{|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\).  Continuity of \(f\) at every point means that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\).  Therefore, when \(\eta<\delta\), every element of the set is less than \(\varepsilon\), so its supremum \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is also less than \(\varepsilon\).  As \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, this shows \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\).

question: Explain how the linearity of the Riemann integral follows from the linearity of Riemann sums as the partition norm tends to zero.

question: In the lecture, the Riemann integral of a continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) is defined as the limit of Riemann sums over any sequence of partitions whose norms tend to zero.  Suppose we have two different sequences of partitions \(\{P_n\}\) and \(\{Q_n\}\), both with \(\|P_n\|\to0\) and \(\|Q_n\|\to0\).  Explain why the Riemann integral can be interpreted as the common limit of the Riemann sums for these two sequences, and describe the role of continuity of \(f\) in ensuring that the two limits coincide.
answer: Because \(f\) is continuous on the compact interval \([a,b]\), it is uniformly continuous.  For any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\).  Since \(\|P_n\|\to0\) and \(\|Q_n\|\to0\), eventually every subinterval in both partitions has length \(<\delta\).  Thus the difference between any two Riemann sums (even with different sample points) is bounded by \(\varepsilon\).  Hence the two sequences of Riemann sums converge to the same limit, which is defined as the Riemann integral of \(f\).  The continuity (uniform continuity) of \(f\) guarantees that the oscillation of \(f\) on arbitrarily small subintervals can be made arbitrarily small, ensuring the limits coincide.

Explain how this fact is used to prove the existence of the Riemann integral for \(f\), and why the convergence of \(\omega(\eta)\) to zero is crucial for the argument.
answer: Uniform continuity of \(f\) implies that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\eta>0\) with \(\omega(\eta)<\varepsilon/(b-a)\).  Choosing a partition whose norm is \(<\eta\) makes the oscillation of \(f\) on each subinterval less than \(\varepsilon/(b-a)\).  Consequently the difference between the upper sum \(U(P,f)\) and the lower sum \(L(P,f)\) is bounded by \(\varepsilon\).  Since \(\varepsilon\) is arbitrary, the upper and lower integrals coincide, proving that \(f\) is Riemann integrable.  The fact that \(\omega(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) is precisely what allows us to make the oscillation on each subinterval as small as we wish, which is the key step in the existence proof.

question: In the definition of the Riemann integral, the norm of a partition is defined as the length of the longest subinterval.  Explain how this notion of norm is used to formalize the idea that partitions become "finer and finer", and why the requirement that the norm tends to zero is essential for the convergence of Riemann sums to the integral.
answer: The norm of a partition measures the size of the largest subinterval.  Requiring \(\|P_n\|\to0\) means that every subinterval in the partition becomes arbitrarily small, so the mesh of the partition refines uniformly across the whole interval.  This guarantees that the sample points used in the Riemann sums can approximate the function values on each subinterval with arbitrary precision.  If the norm did not tend to zero, some subintervals could remain large, and the Riemann sums could differ significantly depending on the choice of sample points, preventing convergence to a single value.  Thus the norm condition is essential for the Riemann sums to converge to the integral.

answer: Because every sequence of partitions with norm \(\to 0\) yields the same limit, the value obtained does not depend on the particular partition or the chosen sample points; thus the integral is uniquely defined. question: In the lecture, it was shown that the Riemann sum of a sum of functions equals the sum of the Riemann sums. answer: Because for any partition \(P\) the Riemann sum satisfies \(S_P(f+g)=S_P(f)+S_P(g)\). Taking the limit as the norm of \(P\) tends to zero gives \(\int_a^b (f+g)=\lim_{||P||\to0}S_P(f+g)=\lim_{||P||\to0}S_P(f)+\lim_{||P||\to0}S_P(g)=\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g\).

question: The lecture mentioned that for continuous functions, the modulus of continuity tends to zero as the interval length tends to zero, which is key to proving existence of the Riemann integral. Explain how this property ensures that the upper and lower Riemann sums converge to the same limit, thereby guaranteeing the existence of the integral.
answer: For a continuous \(f\), given \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(|x-y|<\delta\). If a partition has norm \(<\delta\), the difference between its upper and lower sums is bounded by \(\varepsilon(b-a)\). As the norm tends to zero, this difference tends to zero, so the upper and lower integrals coincide, proving the existence of the Riemann integral.

answer: For any \\(\\varepsilon>0\\), choose \\(\\eta>0\\) such that \\(\\omega(\\eta)<\\varepsilon/(b-a)\\). question: Explain how the fact that the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f(\eta)\) tends to zero as \(\eta\to0\) guarantees that any two Riemann sums based on sufficiently fine partitions are arbitrarily close, and why this leads to the existence of the Riemann integral.
answer: Because \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) we can choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(\omega_f(\eta)(b-a)<\varepsilon/2\) whenever \(\eta<\delta\). If two partitions have norms less than \(\delta\), the difference of their Riemann sums is bounded by \(\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}\|)(b-a)+\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}'\|)(b-a)<\varepsilon\). Thus all sufficiently fine Riemann sums lie within an \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood of each other, which is precisely the Cauchy condition needed for convergence to a limit, the Riemann integral.

The bound \(|S(\mathcal{P})-S(\mathcal{P}')|\le\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}\|)(b-a)+\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}'\|)(b-a)\) shows that the difference between two Riemann sums is controlled by the moduli of continuity evaluated at the norms. question: Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) and let \(P\) and \(Q\) be two tagged partitions with norms \(\eta_P\) and \(\eta_Q\), where \(\eta_P\le \eta_Q\). Using the estimate \(|S(P,f)-S(Q,f)|\le \omega_f(\eta_P)(b-a)\), explain why the sequence of Riemann sums \(\{S(P_n,f)\}\) is Cauchy as the norms of \(P_n\) tend to zero.
answer: Because \(\omega_f(\eta_P)(b-a)\) can be made arbitrarily small: for any \(\varepsilon>0\) choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(\omega_f(\delta)(b-a)<\varepsilon\). Then any two partitions with norms \(<\delta\) satisfy \(|S(P,f)-S(Q,f)|<\varepsilon\). Hence the sequence of Riemann sums is Cauchy.

question: Define \(\omega_f(\eta)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\). Explain why \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) for a continuous \(f\), and how this fact is used to bound the difference between Riemann sums when the partition norm is small.
answer: Continuity of \(f\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). Thus for \(\eta<\delta\) the supremum defining \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is bounded by \(\varepsilon\), so \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\). This allows us to bound \(|S(P,f)-S(Q,f)|\le\omega_f(\eta)(b-a)\) and make the difference arbitrarily small when the partition norm \(\eta\) is small.

question: For a partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) with norm \(\eta\), express the total length \(b-a\) as a sum of subinterval lengths \(\Delta x_k\), and explain why each \(\Delta x_k\le\eta\). Discuss how the norm controls the size of the largest subinterval.
answer: The interval \([a,b]\) is the disjoint union of the subintervals \([x_{k-1},x_k]\) of the partition, so \(b-a=\sum_{k=1}^n\Delta x_k\) where \(\Delta x_k=x_k-x_{k-1}\). By definition of the norm, \(\eta=\max_k\Delta x_k\), hence each \(\Delta x_k\le\eta\). Thus the norm bounds the length of the largest subinterval and controls how fine the partition is.

Visually, each term corresponds to the area of a rectangle whose height is \(f(x_i^*)\) and width \(\Delta x_i\). When the partition is refined—i.e., the subintervals become smaller—the rectangles fit the graph more closely, reducing the over‑ or under‑estimation of the true area. As the norm (the longest subinterval length) tends to zero, the sum of rectangle areas converges to the exact area under the graph, which is the Riemann integral.

question: In the lecture, the main theorem states that for a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\) there exists a unique real number \(\displaystyle \int_A^B f(x)\,dx\) such that for every sequence of partitions \(\{X_R\}\) with \(\|X_R\|\to 0\), the corresponding Riemann sums converge to this number. answer: Continuity of \(f\) on the closed interval \([A,B]\) implies that \(f\) is bounded and, by the Heine–Cantor theorem, uniformly continuous. Uniform continuity guarantees that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a \(\delta>0\) such that whenever \(|x-y|<\delta\), we have \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). When the norm \(\|X_R\|\) of a partition becomes smaller than \(\delta\), the oscillation of \(f\) on each subinterval is less than \(\varepsilon\). Consequently, the difference between any two Riemann sums for the same partition (using different sample points) is bounded by \(\varepsilon(B-A)\). This shows that the set of Riemann sums for partitions with sufficiently small norm is Cauchy, hence convergent. Because the limit does not depend on the particular choice of sample points or on the particular sequence of partitions (as long as the norms tend to zero), the limit is unique. Thus continuity ensures both existence and uniqueness of the limit of Riemann sums.

question: What key property of Riemann sums is used to prove that \(\displaystyle \int (\alpha f+g)=\alpha\int f+\int g\), and how does taking the limit of the sums complete the argument?

question: In the lecture, a continuous function that is differentiable nowhere was constructed. Explain why, for such a function, the derivative does not exist at any point, yet its integral can still be defined. What does this illustrate about the relative smoothness of integration versus differentiation?
answer: For a continuous function \(f\) that is nowhere differentiable, the limit defining the derivative \(f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\) fails to exist at every point \(x\). This failure occurs because the oscillations of \(f\) are too wild for the difference quotient to settle to a single value. However, the Riemann (or Lebesgue) integral of \(f\) over any closed interval \([a,b]\) exists because \(f\) is continuous, and a continuous function on a compact interval is bounded and uniformly continuous, guaranteeing the existence of the integral. Thus, even though differentiation cannot be performed anywhere on \(f\), integration can be performed everywhere. This contrast shows that integration is a smoother operation: it always yields a result for continuous functions, whereas differentiation can fail even for the simplest class of functions.

question: If a sequence \((x_n)\) satisfies \(|x_n-c|\to 0\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), explain why \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\to 0\), and how this fact is used to argue that the difference quotient cannot converge to a finite limit, thereby proving that the function is nowhere differentiable.
answer: Since \(|x_n-c|\to 0\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), we have \(f(x_n)\to f(c)\), so \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\to 0\). If the difference quotient converged to a finite limit, the sequence \(\left|\frac{f(x_n)-f(c)}{x_n-c}\right|\) would be bounded, contradicting the unbounded lower bound derived earlier. Hence the quotient cannot converge, proving the function is nowhere differentiable.

question: The lecture discusses that \(f\) is continuous and bounded. Using the definition of limit, explain why for any sequence \((x_n)\) converging to a point \(c\), the sequence \((f(x_n))\) converges to \(f(c)\).
answer: Continuity at \(c\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-c|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\). Since \(x_n\to c\), for large \(n\) we have \(|x_n-c|<\delta\), hence \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\). Thus \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)=f(c)\).

question: Given the precise definition of continuity at a point \(c\) as \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\), analyze why the converse of "differentiability at \(c\) implies continuity at \(c\)" does not hold in general.
answer: The definition of continuity requires only that the function values approach the function value at \(c\). Differentiability, on the other hand, requires the existence of the limit of the difference quotient \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\). Continuity does not impose any condition on the behavior of this quotient, so a continuous function may have a sharp corner or cusp where the quotient limit does not exist. Hence the converse fails.

question: Considering the definition of a limit as the value a function approaches, discuss why the existence of \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\) (i.e., continuity) does not guarantee that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\) exists, thereby invalidating the converse of the differentiability‑implies‑continuity theorem.
answer: The limit \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\) guarantees that the function values settle at \(f(c)\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\). But differentiability demands that the scaled difference \(\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\) also stabilizes to a finite value. Continuity alone does not control the rate of change of \(f\) near \(c\); the quotient can oscillate or diverge even when the function itself is continuous. Thus the existence of the continuity limit does not imply the existence of the derivative limit, invalidating the converse.

question: The proof uses the inequality \(|\cos(160k x_n)-\cos(160k c)|\le 160k\,|x_n-c|\). Using the definition of absolute value, justify why this bound holds and how it contributes to showing \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}|f(x_n)-f(c)|=0\).
answer: The absolute value measures the distance between two real numbers. Since \(|\cos a-\cos b|\le |a-b|\) for all real \(a,b\), substituting \(a=160k x_n\) and \(b=160k c\) yields \(|\cos(160k x_n)-\cos(160k c)|\le 160k\,|x_n-c|\). This bound, together with the fact that \(\sum 4^{-k}\) converges, allows the limsup of the difference to be made arbitrarily small, proving continuity.

Explain how the absolute convergence of this series ensures that the function \(f(x)=\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) takes real values for all \(x\), and how the fact that the range of \(g(x)\) is \([-1,1]\) helps establish that \(f\) is bounded by a real number.
answer: Because each term \(\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) is a real number and the series of absolute values \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{|\cos(160k\,x)|}{4^{k}}\) converges (since \(|\cos|\le 1\) and \(\sum 1/4^{k}=4/3\)), the sum \(f(x)\) converges to a real limit for every real \(x\). The mapping property of \(g(x)=\cos(kx)\) guarantees that every term lies in \([-1,1]\), so the partial sums are bounded by \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}1/4^{k}=4/3\). Thus \(f(x)\) is a real‑valued function bounded above by the real number \(4/3\).

question: In the lecture, the derivative of \(f(x)=\alpha x^n\) was shown to exist at every point \(c\) in an interval \(I\). Explain how the definition of derivative leads to the formula \(f'(c)=n\,\alpha\,c^{\,n-1}\) and why this holds regardless of whether \(I\) is open, closed, or unbounded.
answer:
The derivative at a point \(c\) is defined as the limit
\[
 f'(c)=\lim_{x	o c} rac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\,.
\]
For \(f(x)=\alpha x^n\) we compute the difference quotient:
\[
 rac{\alpha x^n-\alpha c^n}{x-c}=\alpha\, rac{x^n-c^n}{x-c}\,.
\]
Using the factorisation \(x^n-c^n=(x-c)(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}c+\dots+xc^{n-2}+c^{n-1})\), the quotient simplifies to
\[
\alpha igl(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}c+\dots+xc^{n-2}+c^{n-1} igr).
\]
Taking the limit as \(x	o c\) replaces each \(x\) in the sum by \(c\), yielding
\[
\alpha igl(n\,c^{\,n-1} igr)=n\,\alpha\,c^{\,n-1}.
\]
Thus the limit exists for every real \(c\), so \(f\) is differentiable at every point of any interval \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\), whether \(I\) is open, closed, or unbounded. The polynomial \(f\) is continuous everywhere, and the algebraic simplification shows the limit is independent of the interval’s endpoints, guaranteeing differentiability throughout \(I\).
